extracted.intended_audience: aspiring English orators, preachers, travel-writers, and general readers/interested authors
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on English public speaking (bar, parliament, pulpit, and stage), the appropriate use of gesture and action, and criteria for good travel-writing and general authorship. Emphasises when physical action is useful, the value of native literature, and how a traveller should aim to instruct or please.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of physical action in English public speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a complaint ... that English oratory, however forcible in argument, or elegant in expression, is deficient ... because our speakers want the grace and energy of action. Yet ... I have been hitherto inclined to doubt whether my countrymen are not blamed too hastily for their calm and motionless utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume elaborate gestures will improve English public speaking. In forums intent on truth (the bar, parliament, church), credible testimony and cogent argument outweigh 'laboured gesticulation' or theatrical contortions. Demonstrable benefit, not imitation of foreign mannerisms, should justify adopting more action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of gesture in the pulpit
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether action may not be yet of use in churches, where the preacher addresses a mingled audience, may deserve inquiry. It is certain that the senses are more powerful as the reason is weaker; and that he whose ears convey little to his mind, may sometimes listen with his eyes ... In the pulpit little action can be proper, for action can illustrate nothing but that to which it may be referred by nature or by custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gesture in preaching only to reach the ignorant or rude who respond more to sense than reason; gestures should illustrate by natural similitude or customary allusion (e.g., imitating a motion described, or laying a hand on the breast to express pity). Avoid vague, indeterminate action that settles into habitual peculiarities and becomes ridiculous. Propriety of persuasion (conversion of sinners) outweighs elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage action must be varied, proper, and is not transferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon the English stage there is no want of action; but the difficulty of making it at once various and proper, and its perpetual tendency to become ridiculous, notwithstanding all the advantages which art and show ... may prove how little it can be admitted into any other place, where it can have no recommendation but from truth and nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that theatrical gestures are acceptable onstage but hard to make fitting and risk ridicule. Do not transplant stage mannerisms wholesale into other forms of public address where they lack natural justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument and testimony over modulation and contortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon men intent only upon truth, the arm of an orator has little power; a credible testimony, or a cogent argument will overcome all the art of modulation, and all the violence of contortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise clarity, credibility, and sound reasoning in oratory. Rhetorical showmanship cannot substitute for solid evidence or logical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adopt foreign customs without proving benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs are not to be changed but for better. Let those who desire to reform us show the benefits of the change proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of copying foreign speech mannerisms or literary fashions; reform habits only when clear advantages are demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer native (English) literature for general readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man is more speedily instructed by his own language, than by any other; before we search the rest of the world for teachers, let us try whether we may not spare our trouble by finding them at home. The riches of the English language are much greater than they are commonly supposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For amusement or domestic/household usefulness, consult English authors first. Many useful and valuable English books are neglected; native-language study is often more efficient for general readers than recourse to foreign works.

rubrics_metrics.name: English-language sufficiency across liberal arts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is, I think, not one of the liberal arts which may not be competently learned in the English language. He that searches after mathematical knowledge may busy himself among his own countrymen ... He that is delighted with experiments ... is happily placed where the mechanical philosophy was first established ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that mathematics, natural philosophy, philology, criticism, and other liberal arts have adequate English resources—seek instruction locally where competent writers exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of English divines and sermons for moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: But our own language has, from the Reformation to the present time, been chiefly dignified and adorned by the works of our divines ... No vulgar language can boast such treasures of theological knowledge ... Of morality little is necessary to be said, because it is comprehended in practical divinity, and is, perhaps, better taught in English sermons than in any other books, ancient and modern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For moral teaching and practical divinity, favour English sermons and theological writings as exemplary resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel-writing should instruct, please, or both
rubrics_metrics.description: Every writer of travels should consider, that, like all other authors, he undertakes either to instruct or please, or to mingle pleasure with instruction. He that instructs must offer to the mind something to be imitated, or something to be avoided; he that pleases must offer new images to his reader, and enable him to form a tacit comparison of his own state with that of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your travel account aims to instruct (provide models or warnings), to please (provide striking images and comparisons), or to combine both. Structure and selection of content should serve the chosen purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure travelling method supplies distinct material
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater part of travellers tell nothing, because their method of travelling supplies them with nothing to be told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a method of travel (focus, purpose, observations) that yields significant, reportable material. Avoid publishing bland, generic itineraries that produce no distinct insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial duty: selection, regularity, and avoiding needless multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: To him that has moderately stored his mind with images, few writers afford any novelty, or what little they have to add to the common stock of learning, is so buried in the mass of general notions ... There are indeed some repetitions always lawful ... The author of a system, whether moral or physical, is obliged to nothing beyond care of selection and regularity of disposition. But there are others who claim the name of authors merely to disgrace it, and fill the world with volumes only to bury letters in their own rubbish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing works (histories, systems, natural histories), ensure careful selection of material and orderly arrangement. Avoid contributing redundant publications or trivial repetitions; lawful repetition is limited to cases (history, systematizing) where method, style, or arrangement adds genuine value.
